claim: Multimerized peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) labeling has been the gold standard tool for capturing antigen-specific T cells from a polyclonal repertoire.
source: Multimerized peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) labeling has been the gold standard tool for capturing antigen-specific T cells from a polyclonal repertoire (Jenkins et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jenkins et al., 2010

claim: Tetramers have limitations in monitoring dynamic interactions of antigen-specific T cells in real-time due to their blocking effect on the immune synapse.
source: However, such multimers, most commonly tetramers, have limitations in monitoring dynamic interactions of antigen-specific T cells in real-time due to their blocking effect on the immune synapse.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about tetramer properties and their effects on immune synapses

claim: T cell receptor-like (TCRL) antibodies that detect pMHC complexes are known to disrupt the immune synapse.
source: Likewise, currently available T cell receptor-like (TCRL), also known as peptide-in-groove (PIG), antibodies that detect pMHC complexes are known to disrupt the immune synapse, making them unsuitable for real-time monitoring of antigen-specific T cell interactions (Dahan and Reiter, 2012; Høydahl et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dahan and Reiter, 2012 and Høydahl et al., 2019

claim: Alternative approaches for labeling antigenic peptides with conventional tags have limitations such as size constraints, membrane impermeability, and photophysically unstable nature.
source: Although alternative approaches for labeling antigenic peptides with conventional tags such as fluorescent proteins, fluorophores, and biotin-streptavidin have been used, these tags have limitations such as size constraints, membrane impermeability, and photophysically unstable nature, which restrict their use in applications for dynamic monitoring (Giepmans et al., 2006; Hoffmann et al., 2010; Toseland, 2013; Liu and Cui, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations describing limitations of conventional labeling approaches

claim: The authors developed a labeling strategy involving a six-amino acid tetracysteine tag (CCPGCC) on antigenic peptides that induces fluorescence using membrane permeable thiol-reactive Arsenical Hairpin (AsH) probes.
source: Our approach involves introducing a six-amino acid tetracysteine tag (CCPGCC) on antigenic peptides and inducing fluorescence using membrane permeable thiol-reactive Arsenical Hairpin (AsH) probes (Hoffmann et al., 2010; Adams et al., 2002).
evidence: Describes the methodology developed in this study, with citations to prior work on AsH probes

claim: The OVA(323-339) peptide was engineered by placing the tetracysteine tag at either the amino or the carboxy terminus, away from the TCR and MHC binding sites.
source: We have engineered the OVA(323-339) peptide by placing the tetracysteine tag at either the amino or the carboxy terminus, away from the TCR and MHC binding sites, to avoid disrupting T cell- APC synapse in vitro and in vivo (Robertson et al., 2000).
evidence: Describes experimental design with citation to Robertson et al., 2000 for binding site information

claim: The labeling strategy preserves the T cell priming ability and allows for the detection of the fluorescent signal on the surface of APCs in an MHCII-dependent manner.
source: Owing to these modifications, our labeling strategy preserves the T cell priming ability and allows for the detection of the fluorescent signal on the surface of APCs in an MHCII-dependent manner.
evidence: Describes experimental findings from the study

claim: The labeled peptide is readily taken up by cognate CD4+ T cells with precise specificity in vivo.
source: Using flow cytometry and live microscopy, we found that the labeled peptide is readily taken up by the cognate CD4+ T cells with precise specificity in vivo, as previously shown for pMHC complexes taken up from the immune synapse via processes such as trogocytosis and transendocytosis (Aucher et al., 2008; Daubeuf et al., 2006; Wetzel et al., 2005; Hudrisier et al., 2001; Huang et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from flow cytometry and microscopy, with citations to prior work on trogocytosis

claim: pMHC complexes are taken up from the immune synapse via processes such as trogocytosis and transendocytosis.
source: as previously shown for pMHC complexes taken up from the immune synapse via processes such as trogocytosis and transendocytosis (Aucher et al., 2008; Daubeuf et al., 2006; Wetzel et al., 2005; Hudrisier et al., 2001; Huang et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: The CACA-variant peptide combination induced a distinguished fluorescent signal compared to other tested variants.
source: Flow cytometry analysis showed that CACA- peptide combination but not the other tested variants induced a distinguished fluorescent signal (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1b

claim: Pre-treating OVACACA with tris-2-carboxyethylphosphine (TCEP) blocks cystine disulfide bridge formation and elicits a consistent FlAsH signal.
source: We addressed this problem by pre-treating OVACACA with tris-2-carboxyethylphosphine (TCEP), an irreversible reducing agent that blocks cystine disulfide bridge formation and elicited a consistent FlAsH signal (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c

claim: Pre-incubation of DCs with ReAsH improved signal-to-noise ratio significantly.
source: Moreover, we used another AsH probe excitable by 561 nm laser, called ReAsH, to occupy non-specific cysteine residues that would otherwise attract FlAsH (Stroffekova et al., 2001). Pre-incubation of DCs with ReAsH improved signal-to-noise ratio significantly (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d, with citation to Stroffekova et al., 2001

claim: New variants with two tetracysteine residues or a longer tetracysteine tag provided FlAsH intensity comparable to the original CACA variant.
source: However, new variants provided FlAsH intensity comparable to the original CACA variant, indicating no additional benefit for longer tags (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e

claim: Proliferation and activation status of OTII T cells were not altered by the presence or placement of the tetracysteine tag.
source: Proliferation and activation status of OTII T cells were not altered by the presence or placement of the tag (Figure 2a–d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a-d

claim: Within the first hours of coculture, OTII T cells established stable contact with OVACACA-pulsed DCs, and FlAsH-labeled peptide gradually concentrated at the contact site.
source: Within the first hours of coculture, OTII T cells established stable contact with OVACACA-pulsed DCs, and FlAsH-labeled peptide gradually concentrated at the contact site (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by live confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2e

claim: At 24 hr after treatment, OTII T cells in the peptide-treated groups exhibited increased volume and a shift towards a less spherical shape, indicative of T cell blasting.
source: At 24 hr after treatment, OTII T cells in the peptide-treated groups exhibited increased volume and a shift towards a less spherical shape, indicative of T cell blasting (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by histocytometry data shown in Figure 2f

claim: The interaction of T cells with OVACACA and native OVA323-339 pulsed DCs resulted in a comparable decrease in T cell motility.
source: Furthermore, the interaction of T cells with OVACACA and native OVA323-339 pulsed DCs resulted in a comparable decrease in T cell motility, suggesting that the tag had no impact on their dynamics in vitro (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g

claim: Adoptively transferred DCs were detectable in the popliteal lymph node 18–24 hr post-transfer and they largely disappeared by 48 hr.
source: As previously demonstrated, adoptively transferred DCs were detectable in the popliteal lymph node 18–24 hr post-transfer and they largely disappeared by 48 hr (Bajénoff et al., 2003; Bousso, 2008; Ingulli et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on DC kinetics after adoptive transfer

claim: FlAsH signal remained stable on DCs for the entire duration DCs were present in the lymph node.
source: FlAsH signal remained stable on DCs for the entire duration DCs were present in the lymph node (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3b

claim: FlAsH was picked up by the cognate OTII T cells, suggestive of an antigen-specific peptide major histocompatibility complex II (pMHCII) trogocytosis in-vivo.
source: Strikingly, FlAsH was picked up by the cognate OTII T cells, suggestive of an antigen-specific peptide major histocompatibility complex II (pMHCII) trogocytosis in-vivo (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3c and d

claim: Antigen-specific transfer was confirmed by OVA-Biotin staining on OTII T cells by fluorochrome-conjugated streptavidin.
source: Antigen-specific transfer was also confirmed by OVA-Biotin staining on OTII T cells by fluorochrome-conjugated streptavidin (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3c and d

claim: Antigen-specific Treg cells trogocytose pMHCII from DC synapse more efficiently than their effector CD4+ T cell counterparts.
source: We had previously shown that antigen-specific Treg cells trogocytose pMHCII from DC synapse more efficiently than their effector CD4 +T cell counterparts (Akkaya et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by Akkaya et al., 2019

claim: iTreg cells cocultured with antigen-pulsed DCs performed greater MHCII trogocytosis than naïve T cells at 18 hr in vitro.
source: While iTreg cells cocultured with antigen-pulsed DCs performed greater MHCII trogocytosis than naïve T cells at 18 hr in vitro, peptide-specific trogocytosis was indiscernible within this time frame (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b

claim: OTII iTreg cells acquired OVACACA and OVA-Biotin, with distinct peptide-specific signal and proliferative response on day 2 post-adoptive transfer.
source: Similar to naïve OTII T cells, OTII iTreg cells acquired OVACACA and OVA-Biotin, with distinct peptide-specific signal and proliferative response on day 2 post-adoptive transfer (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c–f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c-f

claim: Intravital two-photon microscopy of the popliteal lymph node confirmed the antigenicity of OVACACA in vivo by revealing morphological changes compatible with T cell priming such as increased T cell volume and decreased sphericity.
source: Intravital two-photon microscopy of the popliteal lymph node further confirmed the antigenicity of OVACACA in vivo by revealing the morphological changes compatible with T cell priming such as increased T cell volume and decreased sphericity (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 3e

claim: OTII-DC synapses had greater 3D volume and duration and harbored more FlAsH than surrounding regions.
source: OTII-DC synapses had greater 3D volume and duration and harbored more FlAsH than surrounding regions (Figure 3g–h).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3g-h

claim: FlAsH signal was exclusively picked up by OTII T cells imaged, as early as 18 hr.
source: Overall, FlAsH signal was exclusively picked up by OTII T cells imaged, as early as 18 hr (Figure 3i, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3i and Video 1

claim: Both streptavidin and FlAsH signals correlated significantly with MHCII expression.
source: Both streptavidin and FlAsH signals correlated significantly with MHCII expression, providing the strongest signal in DCs, where CD4+ T cells served as a negative control due to lack of MHCII expression in mouse T cells (Schooten et al., 2005; Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citation to Schooten et al., 2005

claim: Mouse CD4+ T cells lack MHCII expression.
source: where CD4+ T cells served as a negative control due to lack of MHCII expression in mouse T cells (Schooten et al., 2005; Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schooten et al., 2005 and experimental data

claim: WT DCs, but not MHCII KO DCs, harbored FlAsH signal after adoptive transfer.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of the draining lymph node demonstrated that WT DCs, but not MHCII KO DCs, harbored FlAsH.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from adoptive transfer experiments

claim: Two-photon microscopy of the lymph node confirmed that FlAsH robustly marks OVACACA-MHCII complexes.
source: Two-photon microscopy of the lymph node further confirmed these findings, indicating that FlAsH robustly marks OVACACA-MHCII complexes (Figure 4e–h).
evidence: Supported by two-photon microscopy data shown in Figure 4e-h

claim: OTII and Eα-specific T cells both acquired PKH-26 from double-pulsed DCs, indicating that they captured DC cell membrane from synapse.
source: Flow cytometry analysis showed that OTII and Eα-specific T cells both acquired PKH-26 from double-pulsed DCs, indicating that they captured DC cell membrane from synapse (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5b

claim: TCR-mediated trogocytosis has previously been described as a feature of the DC-T cell synapse.
source: This process is termed as TCR-mediated trogocytosis and has previously been described as a feature of the DC-T cell synapse (Daubeuf et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daubeuf et al., 2006

claim: FlAsH signal was picked up only by OTII T cells despite both T cell types trogocytosing double-pulsed DC cell membrane, suggesting that FlAsH tracks pMHCII mobility with a high precision.
source: Although both T cell types trogocytosed double-pulsed DC cell membrane, FlAsH signal was picked up only by OTII T cells, suggesting that FlAsH tracks pMHCII mobility with a high precision (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5c

claim: OTII and SMARTA T cells had stable contacts with double-pulsed DCs.
source: Popliteal lymph node microscopy confirmed that OTII and SMARTA T cells had stable contacts with double-pulsed DCs (Figure 5d, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5d and Video 2

claim: SMARTA T cells failed to pick up FlAsH signal despite showing signs of antigen-specific contact such as increased volume, reduced sphericity, and decreased track speed.
source: Similar to Eα-specific T cells, SMARTA also failed to pick up FlAsH signal despite showing signs of antigen-specific contact such as increased volume, reduced sphericity, and decreased track speed (Figure 5e–f).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5e-f

claim: Mutations at residues 331 and 333 of OVA323-339 were previously reported to abolish the binding of OTII TCR to OVA323-339.
source: The mutations at 331 and 333, depicted as variants 1 and 2, respectively, were previously reported to abolish the binding of OTII TCR to OVA323-339 (Robertson et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Robertson et al., 2000

claim: Mutant 335 was shown to elicit the normal proliferative response in vitro.
source: Although the residue 335 is flanked between the core OTII TCR binding residues 333 and 336, mutant 335 was shown to elicit the normal proliferative response in vitro (Robertson et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Robertson et al., 2000

claim: Variants 1 and 2 interrupted T cell priming while variant 3 led to a proliferative response similar to native peptide.
source: In line with earlier observations, variants 1 and 2 interrupted T cell priming while variant 3 led to a proliferative response similar to native peptide (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c-d

claim: TCR-mediated uptake of the FlAsH-labeled pMHCII complexes followed the same pattern as T cell proliferation, with only variant 3 complexes producing a comparable signal to that of OVACACA.
source: TCR-mediated uptake of the FlAsH-labeled pMHCII complexes followed the same pattern and only variant 3 complexes produced a comparable signal to that of OVACACA (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6e

claim: AsH-probe labeling can be a sensitive method to track low affinity/nuanced pMHCII complexes.
source: These suggest that AsH-probe labeling can be a sensitive method to track low affinity/nuanced pMHCII complexes.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results with variant peptides

claim: Tetracysteine tagging has been previously applied in cell biology and virology, mostly limited to cell lines and in vitro studies in immunology-unrelated experimental settings.
source: While tetracysteine tagging has been previously applied in cell biology and virology, these applications have been mostly limited to cell lines and in vitro studies in immunology-unrelated experimental settings (Griffin et al., 1998; Mohl and Roy, 2017; Li et al., 2022; Ng et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on tetracysteine tagging

claim: The technique labels antigenic peptides and tracks pMHCII complexes in primary APCs during their interactions with T cells both in vitro and in vivo.
source: On the other hand, our technique labels antigenic peptides and tracks pMHCII complexes in primary APCs during their interactions with T cells both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: Describes the capabilities of the technique developed in this study

claim: The approach is superior to other strategies for monitoring T cell-DC interactions in the way it robustly targets specific pMHCII complexes in real-time in vivo.
source: Our approach is superior as compared to other strategies for monitoring T cell-DC interactions, in the way it robustly targets specific pMHCII complexes in real-time in vivo.
evidence: Comparative claim based on the study's findings

claim: There is no need for special organisms or genetic modifications, and the technique can easily be expanded to new antigens and T cell-APC pairs from both mice and humans.
source: There is no need for special organisms or genetic modifications, and the technique can easily be expanded to new antigens and T cell-APC pairs from both mice and humans.
evidence: Describes the versatility of the technique

claim: The strategy can be integrated into validation efforts for antigen discovery and utilized in the investigation of the synapses of newly deorphanized human T cells.
source: This strategy can, for instance, be integrated into validation efforts for antigen discovery and utilized in the investigation of the synapses of newly deorphanized human T cells, a largely unexplored area where tools are scarce (Dobson et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2022; Lewis and Peters, 2023; Pogorelyy et al., 2022).
evidence: Describes potential applications with citations to relevant work

claim: The two-part system (tag and FlAsH) carries the added capability of being inducible at different time points to allow for increased flexibility in interrogating pMHCII-TCR interactions over time.
source: Given that is a two-part system (tag and FlAsH), it also carries the added capability of being inducible at different time points to allow for increased flexibility in interrogating pMHCII-TCR interactions over time.
evidence: Describes a feature of the technique

claim: The two-part system introduces a high background due to the non-specific binding of FlAsH to endogenous cysteines.
source: On the other hand, this introduces a high background due to the non-specific binding of FlAsH to endogenous cysteines.
evidence: Describes a limitation of the technique

claim: ReAsH pretreatment strategy successfully improved the signal-to-noise profile for FlAsH.
source: Thus, we implemented a ReAsH pretreatment strategy, successfully improving the signal-to-noise profile for FlAsH.
evidence: Describes experimental optimization

claim: Tetracysteine-tagged peptides can be transferred from DCs to T cells via synaptic processes, such as antigen-specific pMHCII trogocytosis/transendocytosis, marking acceptor T cells for several days.
source: Most important of all, our experiments demonstrate that tetracysteine-tagged peptides can be transferred from DCs to T cells via synaptic processes, such as antigen-specific pMHCII trogocytosis/transendocytosis, marking acceptor T cells for several days.
evidence: Describes key experimental findings

claim: Visualization of tetracysteine-tagged pMHCII can complement tetramers in detecting antigen-specific T cells in vivo.
source: Although the turnover of pMHCII in acceptor T cells and its temporal relationship to the TCR downstream events require further elucidation, our visualization of tetracysteine-tagged pMHCII can complement tetramers in detecting antigen-specific T cells in vivo.
evidence: Describes potential application of the technique

claim: Tetracysteine tagging of pMHCII does not broadly alter or disturb T cell-DC synapse by functional read-outs.
source: Additionally, we show that tetracysteine tagging of pMHCII does not broadly alter or disturb T cell-DC synapse by functional read-outs.
evidence: Describes experimental findings on the impact of the tag

claim: The approach offers an advantage over tetramers in that it is suitable for real-time monitoring of the immune synapse.
source: Although the ratio of peptide-FlAsH conjugates to free peptide in DCs would be needed to support this claim, our approach offers an advantage over tetramers in that it is suitable for real-time monitoring of the immune synapse.
evidence: Comparative claim based on the properties of the technique

claim: Tetracysteine tags can be visualized as electron-dense particles by Transmission Electron Microscopy.
source: Finally, it is worth noting that tetracysteine tags can be visualized as electron-dense particles by Transmission Electron Microscopy (Ellisman et al., 2012; Cortese et al., 2009), providing potential for the detailed investigation of T-DC synapse and subcellular localization of pMHCII complexes.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on TEM visualization of tetracysteine tags

claim: The tetracysteine labeling approach provides a powerful and unique tool to advance our understanding of T cell-APC interactions.
source: In conclusion, the tetracysteine labeling approach described here provides a powerful and unique tool to advance our understanding of T cell-APC interactions, offering new opportunities to investigate the immune response and develop improved immunotherapies.
evidence: Summary statement about the significance of the work

claim: Streptavidin detection of biotinylated peptide is a viable option for quantifying peptide loading on cells.
source: It is worth mentioning that streptavidin detection of biotinylated peptide is a viable option for quantifying peptide loading on cells.
evidence: Describes an alternative method

claim: Size and membrane impermeable nature of streptavidin makes it unsuitable for assays that include live monitoring of the T-DC interaction.
source: However, size and membrane impermeable nature of streptavidin makes it unsuitable for assays that include live monitoring of the T-DC interaction (Dundas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dundas et al., 2013
